Capped Cauchy combination of p-values (the paper's rule)

Source: R/truncated-cauchy.R
riposte_capped_cauchy.Rd

Replaces every p-value above cap by cap and then combines the p-values by Liu and Xie's Cauchy combination: the mean of \(\tan((0.5 - p)\pi)\), referred to the standard Cauchy distribution. This is the rule of Bowers and Burton's code (footnote in Section 4.5 of "A More Powerful Test for Randomized Experiments"), with cap = 0.999. Without a cap one p-value of 1 converts to minus infinity and makes the combined p-value 1 whatever the others are. With the cap it converts to \(\tan(-0.499\pi) = -318\). riposte's default for the large-sample Cauchy and hybrid is instead the truncation of Gui, Jiang, and Wang, which converts a p-value of 1 to -3.08 (riposte_truncated_cauchy()); riposte_test() applies this cap when given cauchy_cap.

Usage

riposte_capped_cauchy(p, cap = 0.999)

Arguments

p

numeric vector of p-values in [0, 1].

cap

the largest p-value that enters the combination, in (0.5, 1]; 0.999 by default. cap = 1 gives Liu and Xie's combination unchanged.

Value

the combined p-value.

Examples

# the seven p-values of the paper's example: uncapped the combination is 1
p <- c(0.0003, 0.15, 0.57, 0.05, 0.81, 0.25, 1)
riposte_capped_cauchy(p)            # 0.0030
#> [1] 0.002969598
riposte_capped_cauchy(p, cap = 1)   # 1
#> [1] 1
riposte_truncated_cauchy(p)         # riposte's default rule: 0.0021
#> [1] 0.002088631
